questions.question: What is a sestina?
questions.correctAnswer: A 39-line poem of six sestets plus a tercet with rotating end-words
questions.explanation: A sestina uses six stanzas of six lines plus a three-line envoi, rotating the same six end-words.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: six words dancing through six stanzas - sestina.

questions.question:
Read this passage from William Shakespeare's Hamlet (c. 1603), Act III, Scene I - Hamlet's soliloquy:

"To be, or not to be: that is the question:
Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer
The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,
Or to take arms against a sea of troubles,
And by opposing end them? To die: to sleep;
No more; and by a sleep to say we end
The heart-ache and the thousand natural shocks
That flesh is heir to, 'tis a consummation
Devoutly to be wish'd. To die, to sleep;
To sleep: perchance to dream: ay, there's the rub;
For in that sleep of death what dreams may come
When we have shuffled off this mortal coil,
Must give us pause: there's the respect
That makes calamity of so long life;
For who would bear the whips and scorns of time,
The oppressor's wrong, the proud man's contumely,
The pangs of despised love, the law's delay,
The insolence of office and the spurns
That patient merit of the unworthy takes,
When he himself might his quietus make
With a bare bodkin? who would fardels bear,
To grunt and sweat under a weary life,
But that the dread of something after death,
The undiscover'd country from whose bourn
No traveller returns, puzzles the will
And makes us rather bear those ills we have
Than fly to others that we know not of?
Thus conscience does make cowards of us all;
And thus the native hue of resolution
Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought,
And enterprises of great pith and moment
With this regard their currents turn awry,
And lose the name of action. Soft you now!
The fair Ophelia! Nymph, in thy orisons
Be all my sins remember'd."

The speech turns on the phrase "ay, there's the rub." Before it, Hamlet leans toward death; after it, he argues himself out of it. The turn works because "To sleep: perchance to dream" introduces
questions.correctAnswer: The possibility that death is not blank rest at all, but a state whose unknown contents might be worse than life's known ills
distractors: Proof that the dead are certainly punished for their sins
A memory of Ophelia that distracts Hamlet from his argument
The discovery that ending his life would be physically difficult
questions.explanation: A rub is an obstacle in the path. The obstacle here is knowledge: sleep might contain dreams, death might contain experience, and "in that sleep of death what dreams may come... Must give us pause." Everything after - the catalogue of life's whips and scorns, the undiscovered country, the cowardice of conscience - is built on that single crack in the sleep metaphor.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One word - perchance - stops the whole argument and reverses it.

questions.question: How do tone and mood differ in literature?
questions.correctAnswer: Tone is the author's attitude; mood is the readers feeling
questions.explanation: Tone reflects the author's attitude toward the subject, while mood is the emotional atmosphere the reader experiences.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: author feels tone, reader feels mood.

questions.question: What is anaphora?

questions.question:
Read this passage from William Shakespeare's Hamlet (c. 1603), Act III, Scene I - Hamlet's soliloquy:

"To be, or not to be: that is the question:
Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer
The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,
Or to take arms against a sea of troubles,
And by opposing end them? To die: to sleep;
No more; and by a sleep to say we end
The heart-ache and the thousand natural shocks
That flesh is heir to, 'tis a consummation
Devoutly to be wish'd. To die, to sleep;
To sleep: perchance to dream: ay, there's the rub;
For in that sleep of death what dreams may come
When we have shuffled off this mortal coil,
Must give us pause: there's the respect
That makes calamity of so long life;
For who would bear the whips and scorns of time,
The oppressor's wrong, the proud man's contumely,
The pangs of despised love, the law's delay,
The insolence of office and the spurns
That patient merit of the unworthy takes,
When he himself might his quietus make
With a bare bodkin? who would fardels bear,
To grunt and sweat under a weary life,
But that the dread of something after death,
The undiscover'd country from whose bourn
No traveller returns, puzzles the will
And makes us rather bear those ills we have
Than fly to others that we know not of?
Thus conscience does make cowards of us all;
And thus the native hue of resolution
Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought,
And enterprises of great pith and moment
With this regard their currents turn awry,
And lose the name of action. Soft you now!
The fair Ophelia! Nymph, in thy orisons
Be all my sins remember'd."

The closing movement - "Thus conscience does make cowards of us all; / And thus the native hue of resolution / Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought" - completes the speech's argument by
questions.correctAnswer: Widening Hamlet's private dilemma into a general law: reflection itself drains the will to act, in everyone
distractors: Admitting that Hamlet alone is uniquely cowardly among men
Concluding that death should be chosen after all
Blaming Ophelia's arrival for interrupting a decision
questions.explanation: "Conscience" here means consciousness - thinking itself. The healthy color ("native hue") of resolution turns sickly under thought's "pale cast," and "enterprises of great pith and moment... lose the name of action." What began as one man's question ends as an account of why thought, in anyone, can prevent the very act it contemplates.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The speech ends bigger than Hamlet - thinking itself is the brake.

questions.question:
Read this passage from Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter (1850), Chapter I, "The Prison-Door":

"A throng of bearded men, in sad-colored garments, and gray, steeple-crowned hats, intermixed with women, some wearing hoods and others bareheaded, was assembled in front of a wooden edifice, the door of which was heavily timbered with oak, and studded with iron spikes.

The founders of a new colony, whatever Utopia of human virtue and happiness they might originally project, have invariably recognized it among their earliest practical necessities to allot a portion of the virgin soil as a cemetery, and another portion as the site of a prison. In accordance with this rule, it may safely be assumed that the forefathers of Boston had built the first prison-house somewhere in the vicinity of Cornhill, almost as seasonably as they marked out the first burial-ground, on Isaac Johnson's lot, and round about his grave, which subsequently became the nucleus of all the congregated sepulchres in the old churchyard of King's Chapel. Certain it is, that, some fifteen or twenty years after the settlement of the town, the wooden jail was already marked with weather-stains and other indications of age, which gave a yet darker aspect to its beetle-browed and gloomy front. The rust on the ponderous iron-work of its oaken door looked more antique than anything else in the New World. Like all that pertains to crime, it seemed never to have known a youthful era. Before this ugly edifice, and between it and the wheel-track of the street, was a grass-plot, much overgrown with burdock, pigweed, apple-peru, and such unsightly vegetation, which evidently found something congenial in the soil that had so early borne the black flower of civilized society, a prison.

But on one side of the portal, and rooted almost at the threshold, was a wild rose-bush, covered, in this month of June, with its delicate gems, which might be imagined to offer their fragrance and fragile beauty to the prisoner as he went in, and to the condemned criminal as he came forth to his doom, in token that the deep heart of Nature could pity and be kind to him."

In the phrase "the black flower of civilized society, a prison," the metaphor figures the prison as
questions.correctAnswer: The dark blossom that civilization itself naturally grows out of its own soil
distractors: A rare plant that the colonists imported from England
A sign that the colony's gardens were badly neglected
The one beautiful object in an otherwise ugly scene
questions.explanation: The weeds find something congenial in soil that had so early borne the black flower: the prison is cast as the crop, the thing this ground produces. Black keeps the moral darkness of the surrounding imagery while flower makes the prison organic to civilized society - an outgrowth, not an import or an ornament.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A flower is what soil grows - the prison is civilization's own crop.

questions.question:
Read this passage from Oscar Wilde's play The Importance of Being Earnest (1895), Act I:

"Algernon. Did you hear what I was playing, Lane?
Lane. I didn't think it polite to listen, sir.
Algernon. I'm sorry for that, for your sake. I don't play accurately -- any one can play accurately -- but I play with wonderful expression. As far as the piano is concerned, sentiment is my forte. I keep science for Life.

[...]

Jack. I am in love with Gwendolen. I have come up to town expressly to propose to her.
Algernon. I thought you had come up for pleasure? . . . I call that business.
Jack. How utterly unromantic you are!
Algernon. I really don't see anything romantic in proposing. It is very romantic to be in love. But there is nothing romantic about a definite proposal. Why, one may be accepted. One usually is, I believe. Then the excitement is all over. The very essence of romance is uncertainty. If ever I get married, I'll certainly try to forget the fact.

[...]

Algernon. Yes. But why does your aunt call you her uncle? 'From little Cecily, with her fondest love to her dear Uncle Jack.' There is no objection, I admit, to an aunt being a small aunt, but why an aunt, no matter what her size may be, should call her own nephew her uncle, I can't quite make out. Besides, your name isn't Jack at all; it is Ernest.
Jack. It isn't Ernest; it's Jack.
Algernon. You have always told me it was Ernest. I have introduced you to every one as Ernest. You answer to the name of Ernest. You look as if your name was Ernest. You are the most earnest-looking person I ever saw in my life. It is perfectly absurd your saying that your name isn't Ernest. It's on your cards. Here is one of them. 'Mr. Ernest Worthing, B. 4, The Albany.' [...]
Jack. Well, my name is Ernest in town and Jack in the country, and the cigarette case was given to me in the country.

[...]

Jack. In fact it's perfectly ordinary. Old Mr. Thomas Cardew, who adopted me when I was a little boy, made me in his will guardian to his grand-daughter, Miss Cecily Cardew. Cecily, who addresses me as her uncle from motives of respect that you could not possibly appreciate, lives at my place in the country under the charge of her admirable governess, Miss Prism.

[...]

Jack. When one is placed in the position of guardian, one has to adopt a very high moral tone on all subjects. It's one's duty to do so. And as a high moral tone can hardly be said to conduce very much to either one's health or one's happiness, in order to get up to town I have always pretended to have a younger brother of the name of Ernest, who lives in the Albany, and gets into the most dreadful scrapes. That, my dear Algy, is the whole truth pure and simple.
Algernon. The truth is rarely pure and never simple."

Algernon's remark - "I don't play accurately -- any one can play accurately -- but I play with wonderful expression... I keep science for Life" - establishes him from his first lines as a character who
questions.correctAnswer: Values style, effect, and wit above correctness and fact
distractors: Is a serious musician devoted to technical mastery
Is ashamed of his playing and apologizes sincerely for it
Believes scientific accuracy should govern both art and life
questions.explanation: Accuracy is dismissed as common ("any one can"), expression is the boast, and the piano becomes a philosophy: in art, sentiment over science. Lane's deadpan replies underline that this is performance - Algernon is a man who lives by the well-turned line and prizes how things sound over whether they are right.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: For Algernon, how it sounds beats whether it is right.

questions.question: What is zeugma?
questions.correctAnswer: One word governing two others in different senses
questions.explanation: Zeugma yokes two meanings to one verb, as in he took his hat and his leave.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: one word, two jobs - zeugma.

questions.question: What is litotes?
questions.correctAnswer: Deliberate understatement using a negative, like not bad
questions.explanation: Litotes affirms by negating the opposite, as in not unkind for kind.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: saying less to mean more - litotes understates.

Rooted at the prison's threshold, the wild rose-bush functions in the passage chiefly as
questions.correctAnswer: A counter-symbol to the prison: Nature's pity and fragile beauty offered to the prisoner and the condemned alike
distractors: A botanical record proving roses grew wild in old Boston
A warning that the prison walls are about to be overgrown
A decoration the founders planted to soften the jail's front

questions.question: What is a dramatic monologue?

questions.explanation: A dramatic monologue is a lyric poem spoken by a persona to an implied listener, like Browning's My Last Duchess.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: one voice, silent listener - dramatic monologue.
